extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether pre‑filing activities (use, sale, offers, experiments) trigger the 35 U.S.C. 102(b) public use or on‑sale bars and related exceptions (e.g., experimental use, foreign activity). Intended to instruct examiners and inform practitioners on evidentiary and legal factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence relevant to public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the court emphasized included the 'nature of the activity that occurred in public; the public access to and knowledge of the public use; [and] whether there were any confidentiality obligations imposed on persons who observed the use.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use totality of circumstances to evaluate whether activity 'comports with the policies underlying the public use bar.' Example: an exhibition not open to the public, attendee identity checks, escorts, and prohibitions on note‑taking/photographs weigh against finding a public use (Bernhardt). Consider access, knowledge, and confidentiality obligations together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by third parties deriving the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is in public use if the inventor allows another to use the invention 'without limitation, restriction or obligation of secrecy to the inventor.' (In re Smith).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence or absence of a confidentiality agreement is a factor but not determinative; consider time, place, circumstances, and amount of control the inventor retained. Commercial nature of use and on‑sale aspects of contracts can indicate public use (e.g., sale of seeds to growers resulting in public use). Even hidden uses can be public if no secrecy obligation was imposed (Egbert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by independent third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsecret use of an invention by someone unconnected to the inventor may be a 'public use' if it sufficiently 'informs' the public of the invention or a competitor could reasonably ascertain the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A secret use by another inventor may still be public if the inventive details are ascertainable by inspection/analysis of the product sold or publicly displayed (Gillman, Dunlop). If details remain trade secret and are not ascertainable, the use may not be public (W.L. Gore). A device can be prior art if it places claimed features in the public's possession even if other aspects remain confidential (Lockwood). Consider how many employees had access and whether the party educated others about the invention (Chemithon example). If not sufficiently informing, consider 102(f)/102(g) grounds as alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: On‑sale bar general rule (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An impermissible sale occurs if there was a definite sale, or offer to sell, more than 1 year before the effective filing date and the subject matter of the sale/offer fully anticipated the claimed invention or would have rendered it obvious (Ferag; Pfaff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply traditional contract law principles (look to UCC) to determine whether a commercial offer for sale occurred. Pfaff two‑prong test: (1) product is the subject of a commercial offer for sale not primarily for experimental purposes; and (2) the invention is ready for patenting. See Linear Tech., Group One, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'sale'—contract requirement and variants
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale is a contract where the seller agrees 'to give and to pass rights of property' in return for payment or promise to pay; requires a concrete offer and acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditional sales may still bar a patent (sale conditioned on buyer satisfaction is not automatically experimental). A nonprofit sale can bar a patent if it was for commercial exploitation. Even a single sale or offer may be sufficient to bar patentability. An assignment or sale of patent rights alone is not per se a sale of the invention (Moleculon), but certain licenses that effectively transfer the product immediately (e.g., particular software licenses) can trigger the on‑sale bar; distinguish licenses that merely grant marketing/patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buyer independence / related‑party sales
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale or offer for sale must take place between separate entities; where parties are related, whether there is a statutory bar depends on whether the seller so controls the purchaser that the invention remains out of the public’s hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the degree of control the seller exerts over the buyer. Sales between related entities can still be a statutory bar if the purchaser operates independently (Ferag example where parent/child companies still produced a bar because the buyer had unfettered management).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offers for sale—what counts as an offer
rubrics_metrics.description: Only an offer that rises to the level of a commercial offer for sale—one which the other party could make into a binding contract by simple acceptance—constitutes an offer for sale under §102(b). (Group One).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejected or unreceived offer may suffice to create an on‑sale bar. Delivery is not required. Goods need not be on hand at time of offer. However, the communication must include material terms (price, quantities, time/place of delivery, specs); a communication lacking material terms is not an offer in the contract sense (Elan).

rubrics_metrics.name: The invention must be 'ready for patenting' (Pfaff second prong)
rubrics_metrics.description: The on‑sale bar applies when (1) a commercial offer for sale exists and (2) the invention is 'ready for patenting'—satisfied by reduction to practice before the critical date or by drawings/descriptions sufficiently specific to enable one skilled in the art to practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ready for patenting may be shown by detailed drawings/specifications used to produce the product (Invitrogen, Weatherchem). A product offered that inherently possesses each claim limitation triggers the bar even if parties did not recognize it (Abbott Labs, STX). Actual reduction to practice normally requires testing under working conditions demonstrating practical utility. 'Ready for patenting' does not require readiness for satisfactory commercial marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards / objective evidence of sale or offer
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining if a sale/offer occurred, key question: did the inventor sell or offer for sale a product embodying the claimed invention? Objective evidence (contracts, correspondence, memoranda, drawings, abstracts) controls over uncommunicated seller intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objective documentation—orders, confirmations, abstracts identifying vendor and release/installation dates, descriptions, warranties, price terms—to establish a sale/offer. An order acknowledgement or order confirmation containing material terms prior to the critical date can trigger the on‑sale bar even if later delivery or payment occurred after the critical date (Weatherchem, Ferag).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits/declarations can be admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations submitted under 37 CFR 1.131 to swear behind a reference may constitute an admission that an invention was 'complete' more than 1 year before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such affidavits as potential evidence that the invention was complete prior to the critical date; see MPEP § 715.10 and In re Foster, Dart Indus. examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of a process vs sale of know‑how/product
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed process (series of acts/steps) is not sold in the same sense as a claimed product; 'know‑how' may be sold but that transaction is not a sale of the invention within §102(b) unless the process is performed or the product made by the process is sold by the patentee/licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sale of a product made by the claimed process by the patentee or a licensee constitutes a sale of the process; performance of the claimed process for consideration triggers §102(b). Sale of a prior‑art device different from that in the patent that is later used to perform the claimed method does not constitute an on‑sale bar to the process (Poly‑America).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic scope—'in this country' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b) bars, public use or on‑sale activity must take place in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On‑sale bar generally does not apply where manufacture and delivery occur entirely abroad, but substantial prefatory activity in the U.S. or an offer for sale made/originating in the U.S. may suffice to bring the activity within the statute (Robbins, CTS Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use doctrine (permitted activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental use doctrine asks whether the primary purpose of the inventor at the time of the sale/use was to conduct experimentation (i.e., bona fide effort to perfect the invention or ascertain whether it will serve its intended purpose). If the use/sale was experimental, there is no bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentation must be the primary purpose and any commercial exploitation must be merely incidental. Market testing to gauge consumer demand is commercial exploitation, not experimentation. Where commercial exploitation is significant, applicant bears a heavy burden to establish clear and convincing evidence of experimental purpose. Use indicia of subjective intent manifested by objective evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia of commercial exploitation (negating experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain activities are indicia of commercial exploitation and weigh against finding experimental use: preparation of commercial documents (orders, invoices), preparation/distribution of price lists/quotations, display of samples to prospective customers, demonstration of models/prototypes (especially at trade shows), charging admission for use, and advertising/publicity releases/brochures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the degree of commercial exploitation increases, the burden on applicant to show experimental intent increases. Examiners should scrutinize objective factual circumstances surrounding sales/offers. See cited cases (Akron Brass, Cataphote, InterRoyal, In re Theis, etc.). See MPEP §2133.03(e)(4) for further factors indicative of experimental purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent and notice in experimental scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor's secretly held subjective intent to experiment is insufficient when sales occur in an ordinary commercial environment unless objective evidence supports the claim; customers should be made aware of experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where sales are made to ordinary customers and goods are placed outside the inventor's control, objective evidence (disclosures to purchasers, testing records, contemporaneous experimental documentation) is required to rebut a statutory bar. Secret claims of non‑durability or that units are for testing without customer notice are generally unavailing (LaBounty, Paragon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of the invention and end of experimental use
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use ends when the invention is actually reduced to practice; experimental use 'means perfecting or completing an invention to the point of determining that it will work for its intended purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence shows the inventor considered the invention 'complete' prior to the critical date, awaiting external approvals (e.g., Underwriters' Laboratories) will not ordinarily overcome that conclusion. Lack of resulting modifications from alleged experimental activity is evidence (though not conclusive) that the activity was not experimental. Any modifications resulting from experimentation must be features of the claimed invention to be probative.
